title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
editor_models: none for the main patch (uses MIT's published p50c, made with GPT-6 Astra)

headline_result.text: With thinking on, MIT's p50c patch raised Qwen3.5-0.8B from 0.0% to 22.1% (reference frame) and 19.2% to 33.7% (StepGame), while a rank-1 LoRA (0.09% trainable parameters) trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%; but the LoRA adapters collapsed off-target distance tasks from 94%/92% under p50c to 0-2%.

key_claims.claim: Randomly permuting the elements of p50c's weight change (same norm and sparsity) returned accuracy to base level (1-3/128 and 39-40/200), so the gain depends on the edit's structure.
key_claims.quote: The gain of p50c therefore depends on the structure of its edit.

key_claims.claim: The base model's failures were almost all non-terminations (126-127 of 128 reference-frame outputs hit the 32,768-token limit vs 3 for p50c), consistent with p50c repairing looping as in MIT's math result.
key_claims.quote: The patch’s effect on these tasks is thus consistent with the repair of looping reported for mathematics [15].

notes_for_review: An independent test of MIT's public p50c Qwen3.5-0.8B patch on new tasks, with a permutation (same-norm shuffled delta) control, prompting baselines, a thinking-off diagnostic, an Astra re-edit with matched random perturbation, and rank-1/rank-16 LoRA. Budgets are explicitly unequal: LoRA used 7,168 synthetic worked-solution examples (448 suffice), Adam lr 1e-4, 384 steps, while the closed-form edits used a 72-item development subset; p50c is a fixed artifact not tuned to these tasks. The result supports reading p50c as a looping repair: modest on-target gain but no damage to neighbouring skills, whereas LoRA gives near-ceiling target accuracy with severe task take-over.
